questions.question: Explain how the atmosphere is heated, name the four heat-transfer processes, and account for the three types of rainfall with a South African example of each.
questions.expected_answer: The atmosphere is heated from below. Incoming shortwave insolation largely passes through the air; some is reflected by clouds and the surface and some scattered, so only about half reaches the ground. The warmed surface then radiates longwave terrestrial energy upward, and greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb it — which is why temperature falls with height in the troposphere at about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre. The four transfer processes are radiation, energy travelling as waves; conduction, heat passing by contact from the ground to the air touching it; convection, warmed air rising in vertical currents; and advection, heat carried horizontally by wind. All significant rain requires moist air to rise, cool to its dew point and condense, and there are three lifting mechanisms. Convectional rainfall: strong surface heating drives air upward, building afternoon thunderstorms — the Highveld summer storm with lightning and hail. Orographic or relief rainfall: moist air forced up a mountain barrier rains on the windward slope and leaves a rain shadow on the leeward side — the wet seaward face of the Drakensberg against the dry interior, or the arid Little Karoo behind the Cape ranges. Frontal or cyclonic rainfall: warm air forced to rise over cold air along a front — the Western Cape's winter rain from cold fronts off the Southern Ocean.

questions.question: Set out the three types of plate boundary with the landforms each produces, and distinguish folding from faulting using South African and African examples.
questions.expected_answer: At divergent boundaries plates pull apart and magma rises to fill the gap, building mid-ocean ridges such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and, on land, rift valleys. At convergent boundaries plates collide: where ocean meets continent the denser oceanic plate subducts, melts and feeds volcanoes while ranges like the Andes rise; where ocean meets ocean, subduction builds island arcs like Japan; where continent meets continent, neither can sink and the crust crumples into fold mountains like the Himalayas. At transform boundaries plates slide past one another, building no landforms but storing strain released as earthquakes, as on the San Andreas Fault. Folding happens when compression bends rock layers slowly: the upfold is the anticline, the downfold the syncline, and stacked folds form fold mountains — South Africa's Cape Fold Mountains, folded about 300 million years ago. Faulting happens when rock snaps instead of bending: tension produces normal faults and compression reverse faults. A block dropped between two parallel faults forms a graben or rift valley — the East African Rift Valley, where the continent is slowly tearing apart — and a block left standing high is a horst or block mountain.

questions.question: Describe, in words, how to calculate gradient from a 1:50 000 map, how contour patterns reveal landforms, and how a station model and cold front are read on a synoptic chart.
questions.expected_answer: Gradient is vertical rise over horizontal distance in the same units: subtract the lower height from the higher to get the vertical interval, measure the map distance and convert with the scale — on a 1:50 000 sheet 2 centimetres represents 1 kilometre — then divide the distance by the height difference and state the answer as 1 in that number; 200 metres over 4 000 metres is 1 in 20, a gentle slope, while 1 in 8 is steep. Contour lines join points of equal height at a 20 metre interval; they never cross, and close spacing means steep land. Closed circles within circles mark a summit; tightly stacked contours ringing a flat top mark a Karoo-style tabletop hill; a V where contours cross a river points upstream; contours bunched at the top of a slope show a convex slope and bunched at the bottom a concave one; low ground between two summits is a saddle or neck. On the synoptic chart, a station model packs one place's weather into a circle: shading gives cloud cover in eighths, the wind shaft flies with the wind into the station with feathers counting speed in knots, temperature sits upper left and dew point lower left — the two close together meaning near-saturation. Isobars join points of equal pressure in hectopascals around highs and lows. Ahead of a cold front the air is warm with northerly wind and falling pressure; as it passes, temperature drops, wind swings south-westerly, pressure rises and showers follow.
